stem: What is the shape of the result when multiplying a (3×4) matrix by a (4×5) matrix?
explanation_after: Matrix multiply rule: (m×n) × (n×p) = (m×p). The inner dimensions must match (both 4). Result shape is outer dimensions: 3×5. Most PyTorch errors are shape mismatches.

stem: A linear layer takes input x of shape (batch=32, features=128) and weight matrix W of shape (128, 64). What shape is the output x @ W?
explanation_after: (32×128) @ (128×64) = (32×64). The inner 128s cancel. You go from 32 examples with 128 features to 32 examples with 64 features. This is every linear layer in every neural network.

stem: Which Python operator performs matrix multiplication in NumPy and PyTorch?
explanation_after: The @ symbol is Python's matrix multiplication operator (Python 3.5+). result = A @ B. You'll also see torch.matmul(A, B) or np.dot(A, B) — they do the same thing.

stem: What is the shape of the transpose of a matrix with shape (5, 3)?
explanation_after: Transposing swaps rows and columns: a (5, 3) matrix becomes (3, 5). Transposes are used constantly in ML — for example to align dimensions for multiplication, as in X @ W.T inside a linear layer.

stem: For two (2×2) matrices A and B, which correctly distinguishes element-wise multiplication from matrix multiplication?

options.text: A * B multiplies corresponding elements; A @ B computes the matrix product (row·column dot products)
A * B and A @ B always give the same result for square matrices
A * B is matrix multiplication; A @ B is element-wise
Neither operation is defined for matrices

explanation_after: * (or np.multiply) performs Hadamard (element-wise) multiplication — same-shape arrays, each entry multiplied independently. @ (or np.matmul) performs true matrix multiplication — row-by-column dot products. Confusing the two is one of the most common bugs when implementing neural network layers by hand.

stem: A dataset has 1000 examples, each with 20 features, stored as matrix X with shape (1000, 20). A linear regression model has weights w with shape (20, 1). What does X @ w compute, and what is its shape?

options.text: One single prediction for the whole dataset; shape (1,)
A prediction for every example in one matrix multiplication; shape (1000, 1)
It is invalid because X has more rows than w
The sum of all features; shape (20, 1)

explanation_after: (1000×20) @ (20×1) = (1000×1) — the inner 20s cancel, leaving one predicted value per example. This is the entire point of representing a dataset as a matrix: one matrix multiplication computes all 1000 predictions (1000 dot products) simultaneously, instead of looping over each row in Python.

prompt: Using the drink-machine story, explain what a matrix row means and why the number of columns must match the number of inputs.
explanation_after: A matrix is a tidy wall of mixing knobs: each row turns the same inputs into one new result.
